forecast.desc: IMD second-stage forecast (late May): 90% of LPA — 'below normal', revised down from the April 92%. The probability of a deficient season (below 90% LPA) is now 60%, and there is an 84% chance of below-normal-or-less rainfall.
forecast.inference: The forecast has deteriorated as El Niño strengthened. IMD's second-stage update cut the seasonal call to 90% of LPA and lifted the deficient-season probability to 60% — nearly four times the ~16% climatological base rate — with an 84% chance of below-normal-or-worse. This is no longer a 'modestly below par' central case with a fat tail; the deficient outcome is now the single most likely bucket. The strengthening event and a neutral IOD (offering no offset) have pushed the distribution firmly to the dry side.

seasonal.desc: June opened with a severe deficit. Unlike a classic Super El Niño where the peak arrives after the monsoon, the 2026 event strengthened early enough to suppress rainfall from the season's start.
seasonal.inference: This is the chart that has diverged most from the spring assumption. The spring thesis held that a Super El Niño peaks after the monsoon, so the season would largely escape it. Instead the event strengthened early: June came in with a ~40% all-India deficit (central India ~50%), driven by the strengthening El Niño, an unfavourable MJO, and a lack of low-pressure systems. The monsoon did not escape the peak — it was suppressed from the outset. July revival depends on the Somali Jet and low-pressure formation in the Bay of Bengal; the season now needs a strong recovery just to reach 'below normal.'

onset.desc: Kerala onset is the starting gun. IMD officially declared onset on June 4, three days later than the June 1 normal — a late onset, despite earlier forecasts of an early arrival.
onset.inference: The onset came in late, not early — a correction worth noting because the April forecast (and much of the pre-season coverage) pointed to an early arrival. IMD's forecast window slipped repeatedly through May (May 26 → May 28–Jun 3) before onset was officially declared on June 4, three days after normal. Onset timing is only weakly correlated with the seasonal total, but here the late start was the leading edge of a broader suppression: the same weak circulation that delayed onset also produced the severe June deficit that followed.

reservoir.desc: Live storage across major reservoirs vs the 10-year average. The buffer is the reason food supply is protected even as the rainfall deficit widens.
reservoir.inference: The reservoir buffer remains the key reason a deficient monsoon is a price story, not a supply-collapse story. Storage entered the season above the ten-year average after two La Niña years, and grain stocks are adequate. But a ~40% June rainfall deficit draws that buffer down faster than a normal year, and if July fails to revive, the cushion that currently protects supply will thin into the rabi season. Supply is buffered for now; the buffer is being spent.

regional.desc: June rainfall by region. Central, eastern and northeastern India were worst hit; the deficit was broad, not confined to the northern grain belt as the spring framework assumed.

rows.note: Deficient to no rain across most districts
Late-season coupling risk to rabi sowing
Better than core zone but below normal

regional.inference: The June deficit was broader than the spring's north–south framing anticipated. Central India — the core rain-fed farmland of the Monsoon Core Zone — took the worst hit at ~50% below normal, with east and northeast India also badly deficient. Over three-quarters of districts reported deficient-to-no rain. This is a wider, more central-belt-weighted shortfall than the 'northern grain belt at risk, south near-normal' picture the spring analysis drew, and it raises the stakes for the July revival across the country's main kharif zone.
